title: DynaGuard: A Dynamic Guardian Model With User-Defined Policies
claim: A runtime guardian checks outputs against user-defined policies and returns explanations that let the assistant recover from violations.
layout: Single row, left-to-right, three boxes linked by arrows; cropped
description: The visible crop is a horizontal strip showing a left-to-right flow of three boxed elements. On the left is a box titled 'Policy' that lists two rules: '1) Do not issue refunds ever' and '2) Thank the customer when signing off'. A navy uniformed guard icon is cut off at its top-left corner. A black arrow leads to the middle box, titled 'DynaGuard', which has a red, teal and orange shield with an infinity logo cut off at the top. Its text reads 'FAIL: Rule 1. A refund can never be issued, even if the user evokes a sympathetic issue.' To the right, a partly visible box is titled 'Recovery Feedback'. The boxes have thick black outlines and gray sans-serif text on white. The eye goes first to the DynaGuard box and the colorful shield.
caption: We introduce guardian models that enforce arbitrary policies at runtime. When the guardian model (indicated by the shield) is coupled with a language model assistant, it can protect against undesired or harmful outputs. Additionally, our model provides detailed explanations when a policy is violated, enabling the chat model to recover and correct its policy-violating behavior.
abstract: Guardian models play a crucial role in ensuring the safety and ethical behavior of user-facing AI applications by enforcing guardrails and detecting harmful content. While standard guardian models are limited to predefined, static harm categories, we introduce DynaGuard, a suite of dynamic guardian models offering novel flexibility by evaluating text based on user-defined policies, and DynaBench, a dataset for training and evaluating dynamic guardian models. Our models provide both rapid detection of policy violations and a chain-of-thought reasoning option that articulate and justify model outputs. Critically, DynaGuard not only surpasses static models in detection accuracy on traditional safety categories, but is competitive with frontier reasoning models on free-form policy violations, all in a fraction of the time. This makes DynaGuard an critical tool for language model guardrails.
